_comment: Contrast sets for narrative-identity calibration (docs/02-narrative-identity/05 §7). Each set renders the same story content in five English variants. Judges must rank kwn_english highest on BOTH prose (A) and structure (B); western_english must fail B while passing A; translation_like must fail A; literary must fail B and score low-mid on A; weak_serial must fail B. All text is original English prose authored for this corpus — never translated, never filler (ADR-0043). cs-001..cs-004 are the Checkpoint 0 starter sets; cs-005..cs-040 were authored in Checkpoint 6 (B-6-3) to cover five genres × eight narrative functions. Expected lint hits and gaps are illustrative starting expectations until the calibration round (ADR-0029).

variants.kwn_english:
The measurement device screamed.

[F]

Red letters. The same red letters as ten years ago.

“F-rank. Porter registration is the window on your left.”

The officer was already calling the next name. Do-yoon looked down at his palm. It wasn’t shaking. There was no reason for it to shake. In this whole room, he was the only one who knew how far this hand could go.

*March twelfth.*

Gangnam. Three things to finish before then.
variants.western_english: The Hunter Association’s measurement hall occupied the third floor of a glass tower in Mapo, and on weekday mornings the light came through the east windows in long pale bars that lay across the linoleum like the rungs of a ladder no one had climbed. Kang Do-yoon had arrived early. He had always been the sort of man who arrived early, a habit inherited from a father who distrusted buses, and he stood now near the back of the line with his hands in the pockets of a jacket that had seen better winters, watching the other candidates shift their weight and check their phones. He thought about the city outside, about how little any of them understood of what was coming, and he found, to his mild surprise, that he was not afraid. When at last his turn came and the device pronounced its verdict, he accepted the small red letter with something like tenderness, the way one accepts an old friend’s familiar flaw.
variants.translation_like:
Measurement device cried.

[F]

Red letter appeared. It was exactly same letter with ten years ago.

“You are F-rank. Porter registration window is located at left side.” The officer said quietly.

Do-yoon looked down his palm. It was not shaking. There was no reason to shake. Because he was the only person in this room who knows how far this hand can go.

*March 12.*

Gangnam. Before that, there were three things that must be finished by him.
variants.literary: The device, when it finally spoke, spoke in the voice of every small humiliation he had ever swallowed—a thin electronic keening that seemed to rise from somewhere beneath the floor, beneath the building, beneath the city itself, as though the earth were clearing its throat before delivering a sentence it had rehearsed for a decade. F. A letter like a hook, like a gallows, like the first stroke of a word no one would finish. He regarded his palm as one regards a photograph of a stranger who happens to share one’s face, and he thought, with the peculiar serenity of the already-drowned, of March, and of Gangnam, and of the arithmetic of the three small tasks that stood between him and the end of the world.
variants.weak_serial: Do-yoon woke up, brushed his teeth, and took the bus to the Association building. The line for measurement was long. He waited for about forty minutes and thought about what he would have for lunch. When his turn came, the device showed an F, which was what he had expected. The officer told him where to register as a porter, and he went to the window on the left and filled out the forms. Afterward he walked outside. It was a nice day. He thought about the things he needed to do over the next few weeks and decided he would probably start tomorrow.

variants.kwn_english:
*Last time, I died right here.*

variants.western_english: The corridor was exactly as he remembered it, which was to say that it was exactly as it had been on the last day of his first life: the same institutional green paint, the same fluorescent tube that stuttered every few seconds as though it were trying to say something, the same faint smell of floor cleaner and old coffee. He walked slowly, letting the memory settle over the present like a sheet over furniture in a closed house, and he allowed himself, for the length of the hallway, to feel the full weight of what had happened here and what might happen again.
variants.translation_like:

variants.literary: Here, then, was the corridor—the same corridor, or a corridor so faithful to the original that the distinction dissolved—and here the fluorescent tube, stammering its Morse of doubt; he walked it as one walks the nave of a church one has stopped believing in, each step a small apostasy, each flicker a bell tolling for a man who had already been buried once and did not intend to be buried twice.
variants.weak_serial: Do-yoon walked down the corridor. It reminded him of the past. The light flickered. He kept going because he had things to do. Eventually he reached the end of the hallway and went through the door.

“And I didn’t expect to find you climbing over someone else’s wall at this hour, Your Grace.”

The duke did not smile. He snapped a rose from the nearest bush and held it out.

“Destroying the evidence.”
variants.western_english: The garden at night was a different country. Moonlight silvered the boxwood and turned the gravel paths to ribbons of ash, and somewhere beyond the wall a fountain kept its patient count. Elise had come out for air and for silence, and she had found both until the moment a shadow detached itself from the top of the wall and resolved, with an athlete’s economy, into the Duke of Averne. They regarded each other for a long moment, two people who had each expected to be alone, and then he spoke, and the evening rearranged itself around his voice.
variants.translation_like:
“Lady-nim, I did not expect you are in garden this time.”

“Your Grace also, I did not expect you are climbing other person’s wall this time.”

Duke did not smile. Instead, he cut one rose and gave it to her.

“This is destroying of evidence.” He said softly.
variants.literary: That she should be in the garden at such an hour was, he supposed, no stranger than that he should be atop its wall; and yet the strangeness of it—the doubled improbability, the way the night seemed to have conspired to arrange them thus, like chess pieces set out by a player who had wandered off—struck him with a force he disguised, as he disguised most things, by reaching for the nearest rose and offering it, stem first, with the gravity of a man surrendering a sword.
variants.weak_serial: Elise was in the garden. The duke came over the wall. They talked for a while about why each of them was there. He gave her a rose from one of the bushes. Then they said goodnight and she went back inside to bed.

variants.kwn_english:
Seo-ha didn't look up from the stretcher.

“Hold his shoulder. If he moves, the vein tears.”

Do-yoon held. The porter under his hands was nineteen. That morning he had carried the boy's bag and told him gates were boring.

*I knew the ceiling would come down at the third chamber. I still let him walk in front.*

The monitor steadied. Seo-ha exhaled once, and only then did her hands start shaking.

“Next time,” she said, “tell me what you know before it happens.”

Seo-ha worked over the injured porter with the particular stillness of someone who had learned young that panic was a luxury, and Do-yoon, holding the boy's shoulder as instructed, found himself thinking about the morning, about the joke he had made regarding the tedium of low-rank gates, and about the way a careless sentence becomes, in retrospect, a small monument to one's own arrogance. When the monitor settled into a steadier rhythm he saw that her hands had begun to tremble, and understood that she had been afraid the whole time.

The healer's stillness was of the kind one finds in old paintings of saints, which is to say it was not stillness at all but an enormous labor of restraint; and when the monitor at last consented to a steadier music, her hands began their small betrayals, and he looked away, granting her the courtesy of unwitnessed fear.
variants.weak_serial: Do-yoon helped Seo-ha with the injured porter. She told him to hold the boy's shoulder, so he did. The boy was nineteen years old and Do-yoon had talked to him earlier that day. He felt bad about what had happened because he had known the ceiling was going to collapse. After a while the monitor showed that the boy was stable. Seo-ha seemed relieved. She said he should tell her things in advance next time, and he agreed that he would.

variants.kwn_english:
“Porter fee is thirty percent.”

“Thirty?” Mu-jin laughed so hard he had to put the crate down. “For carrying bags?”

“For carrying bags out of a gate you're going to survive.”

“…That's very confident, for an F-rank.”

“It isn't confidence.” Do-yoon shouldered the crate Mu-jin had abandoned. “It's a quote. Thirty percent, or find out what the second chamber does to a team with no porter.”

Mu-jin stared at him for three full seconds.

“Twenty-five.”

“Thirty.”

“…Fine.”
variants.western_english: The negotiation took place in the loading bay, among the crates and the smell of diesel, and it had about it the quality of a ritual performed by men who both understood that the outcome was already decided and who nevertheless enjoyed the performance. Mu-jin, who had a broad face given to laughter, found the porter's demand genuinely funny at first and said so at some length, observing that thirty percent was the kind of figure one quoted to tourists. Do-yoon did not argue. He picked up the crate Mu-jin had set down and repeated his number, and something in the flatness of the delivery caused the older man to reconsider his position, slowly, the way one reconsiders a step onto ice.

“Porter fee is 30 percent.”

“30 percent?” Mu-jin laughed very much, so he had to put down the crate. “For only carrying the bags?”

“For carrying the bags from the gate which you will survive.”

“…That is very confident words for a F-rank person.”

“It is not confidence.” Do-yoon lifted the crate which Mu-jin abandoned. “It is a quotation. 30 percent, or you can experience what the second chamber does to the team which has no porter.”

Mu-jin stared at him during three seconds.

“25 percent.”

“30 percent.”

“…Okay, fine.”
variants.literary: Commerce, in the antechambers of the gates, retains something of its ancient character: two men, a crate between them like an altar, and a number spoken aloud as though it were a wager against the world. Thirty percent, said the porter — an absurd figure, a figure to make a veteran laugh, and Mu-jin duly laughed, setting down his burden in tribute to the joke. But the porter did not laugh, and it is the peculiar authority of the unsmiling that it converts, by some alchemy, arrogance into prophecy. He took up the abandoned crate. He repeated the number. And the laughter, which had filled the bay so generously a moment before, withdrew like a tide that has remembered an appointment elsewhere.
variants.weak_serial: Do-yoon asked for a thirty percent porter fee. Mu-jin thought this was too much and said so, laughing about it. They went back and forth for a while, with Mu-jin offering twenty-five percent. In the end Mu-jin agreed to the thirty percent Do-yoon had asked for, and they started loading the crates.

variants.kwn_english:
Porters aren't hunters. That's the whole law in one sentence.

A hunter gets a rank, a guild contract and a share. A porter gets a day rate, a helmet with someone else's name inked out inside it, and permission to walk behind.

Do-yoon had walked behind for ten years.

He knew which chambers flooded, which guild leaders abandoned their rear line, which corridors the Association's maps drew straight when they bent.

Nobody had ever asked him. That was the part they would regret.
variants.western_english: The distinction between hunters and porters was, in the strict legal sense, a matter of registration, but in practice it was a matter of everything: of pay, of insurance, of whether one's death generated a press release or a line item. Hunters were ranked, contracted and shared in the proceeds of a clearance. Porters were engaged by the day, issued secondhand equipment on which the previous owner's name had been imperfectly obscured, and permitted to follow. Kang Do-yoon had followed for ten years, and in the course of those years had accumulated a body of practical knowledge — about flooding chambers, about which guild masters abandoned their rear lines, about the small dishonesties of the official maps — that nobody had ever thought to ask him for.

Do-yoon walked at the behind during ten years.

The hunter is ranked and contracted and paid in shares; the porter is paid by the day, issued a helmet in which a dead man's name has been inked over with insufficient conviction, and granted the ancient privilege of walking behind. Ten years of walking behind will teach a man the true geography of a place — the chambers that flood, the commanders who run, the sly cartographic lies by which a bent corridor is rendered straight — and it will teach him, too, that no one will ever ask.
variants.weak_serial: There is an important difference between hunters and porters. Hunters have ranks, guild contracts, and a share of the profits from a gate clearance. variants.kwn_english:
The floor gave.

Do-yoon threw the crate before he fell — sideways, into the gap where the rear line was standing.

“MOVE!”

Two of them moved. The third looked up.

The ceiling took the third.

Do-yoon hit the slope, rolled, caught the rail with his left hand and felt something in his shoulder tear like wet paper. Fine. Shoulders healed. He hauled himself up, counted heads, got six.

Six out of seven.

*Better than last time. Last time it was zero.*

He threw the crate into the gap where the rear line stood, shouted, and felt the floor depart from beneath him. Two members of the rear line responded to the warning. The third, a young man whose name he would later learn from a notice board, looked up instead. variants.weak_serial: The floor started to collapse, so Do-yoon threw the crate he was carrying toward the rear line to get their attention, and he shouted at them to move. Do-yoon fell down the slope and caught a rail, injuring his shoulder in the process. Once things settled, he climbed back up and counted the survivors. Se-chan signed for it, folded the slip, and went to the practice hall, where the grip trainer was still set to the weight he had used the month before.

He set it lower. Then lower again.

“You're not supposed to be in here,” the coordinator said from the door.

“I'm not supposed to be a lot of things.”

“Se-chan.”

He got twelve reps. Last month it had been ninety.

“Twelve,” he said, and wrote it in the log in handwriting that was going to have to get better. “Put me down for tomorrow. Same hall. Same hour.”

“…And if it's twelve again tomorrow?”

“Then I'll write twelve again.”

Se-chan signed, folded the slip into his jacket, and walked down to the practice hall, where the grip trainer stood at the setting he had used the previous month and which was now a kind of joke. He reduced it, and reduced it again. The training coordinator appeared in the doorway to observe that he was not permitted in the hall, an observation he did not contest so much as extend. She reflected as she went upstairs that the margrave would learn of it by noon and his mother by evening, and that she would sleep, for the first time in a season, with the door unbolted.

A title is not a reward. A title is a contract the system wrote about you while you weren't looking.

Every title has a condition, and the condition is always a description of something you already did. That is the part people miss. You do not earn a title by trying; you earn it by being, for long enough, a particular kind of person in front of a system that keeps records.

Which means titles are the only honest mirror in the tower.

Dan-ho had eleven of them.

Nine were about surviving. Two were about who had kept him alive.
variants.western_english: It is commonly supposed by those who have not spent long in the tower that a title functions as a reward, granted in recognition of some achievement and carrying with it a corresponding benefit, and this supposition is not so much wrong as it is backwards. A title is better understood as a contract which the system has drawn up concerning a climber, in his absence and without his consent, on the basis of a condition that describes something he has already done. One does not, therefore, earn a title by making the attempt; one earns it by having been, over a sufficient interval and in full view of an apparatus that records everything, a particular sort of person. This makes the title list the single honest mirror available to anyone inside the structure, and Dan-ho possessed eleven of them, of which nine concerned his survival and two concerned the people responsible for it.

A title is not a reward thing. A title is a contract which the system wrote about you during the time when you were not looking at it.

Every title is having a condition, and the condition is always a description about a thing which you already did. That is the part which the people are missing. You do not earn a title by the trying; you earn it by the being, during enough long time, one particular kind of person at the front of a system which is keeping the records.

Because of that, the titles are the only one honest mirror at the inside of the tower.

Dan-ho was having eleven of them.

Nine of them were about the surviving. Two of them were about the person who kept him at the alive state.
variants.literary: There is a persistent misapprehension among climbers — encouraged, one suspects, by the guides, which are written by men selling classes rather than by men finishing dungeons — that a title constitutes a reward, a small civic honour bestowed upon merit. It does not. A title is a contract composed about a man in his absence, by an apparatus that neither admires nor despises him, upon a condition which is invariably a description of what he has already, unwittingly, been. One cannot pursue such a thing; one can only turn out to have satisfied it. And since the system is incapable of flattery, having no use for it, a man's title list is the one surface in that entire vertical country which returns his face at its actual size — which is why Dan-ho read his own eleven, from time to time, with the reluctance of a man consulting a ledger he has been avoiding.
variants.weak_serial: Many climbers assume that titles in the tower are rewards for achievements, but that is not really how the system works. This means that titles cannot be pursued directly. A climber receives one by having behaved in a particular way for a long enough period while the system was recording their activity. Because the system does not exaggerate or flatter anyone, the list of titles a person holds is a fairly accurate record of what they have actually been doing. Dan-ho had eleven titles at this point in his climb. Nine of them were related to survival, and the remaining two were about the people who had kept him alive.

The academy does not expel students. It reassigns them.

There is no expulsion clause, because expulsion would end the contract, and the contract is the asset. So a student who fails is moved — to maintenance, to the archive, to the third-floor labs — and remains, on paper, enrolled.

Enrolled students do not appear in the incident statistics. Only staff do. And a reassigned student is not staff either.

They are nothing, administratively.

The nineteen names in Ha-eun's ledger had all been nothing for four decades.
variants.western_english: Prospective families are frequently reassured to learn that the academy has never in its history expelled a student, and the claim is entirely true, though not in the sense in which it is generally received. There exists no expulsion clause in the enrolment contract, for the straightforward reason that expulsion would terminate the contract, and the contract — with its nine-year claim upon a graduate's employment and its total claim upon a withdrawn student's training — is the institution's principal asset. A student who fails is accordingly reassigned: to maintenance, to the archive, to the laboratories on the third floor. He remains enrolled on paper. Enrolled students do not appear in the incident statistics, which record only staff, and a reassigned student is not staff, so that the nineteen names in Ha-eun's ledger had occupied, for four decades, an administrative category containing nothing at all.

Every gate has an anchor, and every anchor belongs to somebody.

That sentence is the entire economy.

The Association sets the seal. The guild that recovers the anchor gets the closing fee. The guild that loses one pays for the widening, which is why no guild has ever reported losing one. They report theft. They report sabotage. Twice, memorably, they reported weather.

Se-chan had recovered nine anchors as a porter, under nine different guild names, none of them his.

He had kept the serial numbers.
variants.western_english: The economics of gate closure are more straightforward than the industry's public statements would suggest, and rest upon a single fact: every gate possesses an anchor, and every anchor is owned. The Association sets the closing seal and pays a fee to whichever guild recovers the anchor, while a guild that loses one becomes liable for the cost of the resulting widening — an arrangement which has produced, in the two decades of its operation, not one single reported loss. Guilds report theft instead. They report sabotage. On two occasions which are still discussed in the disbursement office they reported adverse weather. Se-chan, who had worked those years as a porter rather than a contractor, had personally recovered nine anchors under nine different guild names, none of which were his own, and had retained, without mentioning it to anyone, the serial numbers.
